title: You were strangers
hookLine: love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt (Deuteronomy 10:19)

cards: The first week in a new place has its own feel. Nobody tells you which door people actually use, how the bus takes payment, who to ask about the trash. You smile too much, or not enough.
The Torah returns to that position more than once, the newcomer's, and asks its readers to remember standing in it. This first week of the love block ends right there, with the stranger.

teach.b: First, love the stranger. In Deuteronomy, Moses describes God as the one who loves the stranger, giving him food and clothing, and then says: "Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."
The reason isn't an argument. It's a memory.

Second, as thyself, again. Yesterday's chapter, Leviticus nineteen, says the stranger who lives with you shall be as one born among you, "and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."
The love owed to the neighbor is stretched, on purpose, to the outsider.
Third, the heart of a stranger. Exodus puts it plainly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Empathy, in this text, isn't imagination.
It's history carried in the body.
Fourth, the week in one line.

Diotima's ladder, Aristophanes' halves, Aristotle's friends, another self, Montaigne's La Boétie, Leviticus: the week began with one beautiful face and one chosen friend, and came round to the neighbor.
The stranger widens the circle again: someone not chosen, not yet known, whom the Torah asks its readers to welcome anyway.

how: Jewish tradition cites the Torah's command to love the stranger, remembering slavery in Egypt, in teaching about welcoming guests and newcomers, and the memory of Egypt is retold each year at the Passover seder.

games.q: a stranger has come to live among you. what does Leviticus nineteen say to do?
o: keep them at a polite distance.
treat them as one born among you, and love them as yourself.
welcome them once they've become like you.
games.why: "as one born among you," and "thou shalt love him as thyself," because ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

practice: Let a newcomer come to mind: someone new at work, in your building, at your table, in your town. Breathe in and remember a time you were the new one, what you didn't know, who helped and who didn't.
Breathe out and let that memory turn toward them, along with the one thing you wish someone had told you back then.

wordCard.voice: Moses. In Deuteronomy, he gives the reason for loving the stranger: not an argument, but a memory of being one. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the stranger, an outsider living among the people; the word behind love ye the stranger.
